Backtracking

Build an answer one choice at a time, and undo a choice the moment it cannot work. Guide a mouse through a maze, draw decision trees, list subsets and permutations, prune a search, place N queens, solve a Sudoku and trace words on a grid.

Part 1

🐭Backtracking: choose, explore, unchoose

Imagine a mouse in a maze looking for cheese. At every corner it picks a corridor and walks on. If the corridor ends in a wall, it walks back to the last corner and tries the next corridor. That is backtracking: build an answer one choice at a time, and as soon as a choice cannot work, undo it and try another.

1️⃣ Choose

Make one choice and record it: step into a square, put a letter in a seat, place a queen.

2️⃣ Explore

Recurse to make the next choice on top of this one.

3️⃣ Unchoose

Undo the choice exactly, so the next option starts from a clean state.

Backtracking is recursion plus an undo. Whatever you change before the recursive call, change back after it.
Part 2

🌳The decision tree and all subsets

Every backtracking run walks a decision tree. Each level is one decision, each branch is one option, and each leaf is a finished answer. For subsets the decision is simple: for every item, take it or leave it. Three items give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 leaves, one per subset.

🍃 Leaves are answers

A path from the root to a leaf lists the decisions. The number of leaves is the number of answers, here 2n.

📏 Depth is memory

The recursion is only as deep as the tree, n levels, so the extra memory is O(n) even though the tree has 2n leaves.

The Bit manipulation chapter builds the same 2n subsets with a counter and bit masks. Backtracking is the version that lets you stop early, as you will see with pruning.
Part 3

💺Permutations: every possible order

To list every order of a, b and c, fill the seats left to right. Seat 1 can take any of the 3 letters, seat 2 any of the 2 still free, seat 3 the last one. That is 3 × 2 × 1 = 3! = 6 orders. A used list remembers which letters already sit somewhere.

Part 4

✂️Pruning: cut branches that cannot win

A plain search visits every branch. Pruning spots branches that can never lead to an answer and skips them. In Combination Sum we want numbers that add up to a target. If the numbers are sorted and the next one is already bigger than what is left, every number after it is bigger too, so the whole rest of the loop can be cut.

✂️ Common pruning rules

Stop when the running total passes the target. Stop when too few items are left to finish. Skip a value equal to the one just tried, to avoid duplicate answers.

⏱️ Cost

Backtracking is still exponential in the worst case. Good pruning does not change that bound, but in practice it often removes most of the tree.

Part 5

👑N-Queens: a board full of rules

Place n queens on an n by n board so that none can attack another. A queen attacks along its row, its column and both diagonals. Put exactly one queen in each row. For the next row, try each column, skip the attacked squares, and if a row has no safe square left, go back and move the queen in the row above.

🧭 Diagonal keys

All squares on one diagonal share row − col. All squares on one anti diagonal share row + col. Three sets make the attack test O(1).

🙅 No solution is an answer

For 2 and 3 queens the search tries everything and finds nothing. Backtracking then proves there is no solution, which is useful too.

Part 6

🔢Sudoku: fill a square, check, go back

A Sudoku solver is backtracking in its purest form. Find the first empty square, try the digits one by one, and keep the first digit that does not clash with its row, its column or its box. Then solve the rest. If some later square has no digit left, the earlier choice was wrong, so erase it and try the next digit there.

Check a choice as early as possible. Testing the row, column and box before recursing is the pruning that makes Sudoku fast.
Part 7

🔤Searching a grid: word search

Can the word be traced on a board of letters, moving up, down, left or right, without using a square twice? Start on every square that holds the first letter. From there, step to a neighbour holding the next letter, mark the square as used, and continue. If you get stuck, unmark the square and try another neighbour.

The unmark step matters. Without it, a square used by one failed path stays blocked, and a later path that needs it would be missed.
